2027-04-20.title: Tuesday of the Fourth Week of Easter
readings: They spoke to the Hellenists also, proclaiming the Lord Jesus
All you nations, praise the Lord (or: Alleluia)
The Father and I are one
2027-04-20.alt: Easter weekday. The paschal candle burns beside the ambo; the Alleluia returns in the antiphons and the Gospel acclamation; the Regina Caeli (Queen of Heaven) replaces the Angelus until Pentecost. Liturgical colour: white.
2027-04-20.verse: My sheep hear my voice. I know them, and they follow me. I give them eternal life, and they will never perish.
theo: After the martyrdom of Stephen a persecution broke out in Jerusalem, and many believers fled. What looked like a disaster became a sowing. Those who were scattered “traveled as far as Phoenicia, Cyprus, and Antioch,” and wherever they went they spoke the word. At first they spoke only to fellow Jews. Then some men from Cyprus and Cyrene, whose names we do not even know, did something new at Antioch: they “spoke to the Hellenists also, proclaiming the Lord Jesus.” Here the word means Greek-speaking Gentiles. And “the hand of the Lord was with them, and a great number became believers and turned to the Lord.” The first great mission to the Gentiles was not planned by a committee. It was begun by refugees who could not keep silent about Jesus.

The Church in Jerusalem sends Barnabas to see what is happening. Luke gives him one of the finest descriptions in the New Testament: “he was a good man, full of the Holy Spirit and of faith.” When he arrives, he does not look for faults. He “saw the grace of God” and “he rejoiced.” He encourages them to stay faithful. Then he does something humble and wise: he goes to Tarsus to fetch Saul, a converted persecutor whom many still feared, and brings him to Antioch. For a whole year they teach together. And “it was in Antioch that the disciples were first called ‘Christians.’” The name means “Christ's people,” the people who belong to the Anointed One. Antioch, a great city of many nations, became the mother church of the missions. The Psalm sings of Zion as the mother of all peoples: “Glorious things are spoken of you, O city of God,” and of people from Egypt, Babylon, Philistia, Tyre and Ethiopia, it says, “This one was born there.” In the Church, every nation is born again.

The Gospel takes us to the Temple in winter, at the festival of the Dedication, the feast we know as Hanukkah, which remembers the rededication of the Temple after the Maccabees. Jesus is walking in the portico of Solomon. Some of the Temple crowd gather around him: “How long will you keep us in suspense? If you are the Messiah, tell us plainly.” Jesus answers that his works already speak. And then he gives one of the most consoling promises in the Gospel: “My sheep hear my voice. I know them, and they follow me. I give them eternal life, and they will never perish. No one will snatch them out of my hand.” The security of the sheep does not rest on their strength but on the hand that holds them, and that hand is one with the Father's: “no one can snatch it out of the Father's hand. The Father and I are one.” At the feast that celebrated the dedication of the Temple, Jesus reveals himself as the true dwelling of God among us. The Church has always heard in these words the mystery of the Holy Trinity: the Son is one in being with the Father.
conn: The persecution that followed Stephen's death (Acts 8:1–4). Luke shows how God turns the flight of the believers into the spread of the word.
The coast of present-day Lebanon, the island home of Barnabas (Acts 4:36), and Antioch on the Orontes in Syria, the third city of the Roman Empire after Rome and Alexandria.
In Acts 6:1 the word means Greek-speaking Jews; here in Antioch, where the contrast is with “Jews” in verse 19, it means Greek-speaking Gentiles. Some ancient manuscripts read “Greeks.”
Joseph, a Levite from Cyprus, whom the apostles named Barnabas, “son of encouragement” (Acts 4:36). He sold a field and laid the money at the apostles' feet. His feast is 11 June.
From Christos, Messiah, Anointed One. Probably first used by outsiders. St Ignatius, bishop of Antioch around 107, would write that he wanted not only to be called a Christian but to be found one.
Hanukkah, in December, recalling the cleansing and rededication of the Temple by Judas Maccabeus in 164 BC (1 Maccabees 4:36–59). John alone mentions it.

In John's Gospel this phrase often refers to some Temple authorities and their followers who opposed Jesus, not to the Jewish people as a whole. Jesus, his Mother and the apostles were Jews. The Church firmly rejects any blame of the Jewish people for his death (Nostra Aetate 4; Catechism 597).
In Greek the word is neuter: not one person, but one in being and in action. The Council of Nicaea (325) confessed the Son “consubstantial with the Father.”
altar: “No one will snatch them out of my hand.” In Holy Communion the hand of the Shepherd holds us most closely: he places himself in our hands and on our tongue, so that we may be held in his.
The first disciples to be called Christians were those who met for a whole year to be taught. The Mass is the school of Christians: the word explained, the Bread broken, the community gathered.
outline: Ask: what name do people give me, and does it say that I belong to Christ?
Refugees who could not keep silent.
Point 2 · A good man, full of the Spirit
A shepherd's open hand, with a lamb resting in it, and another hand closed around it.
“No one will snatch them out of my hand.”
live: If you have moved for work or study, to the Gulf, to Bengaluru, to Europe, see yourself as one of the scattered ones of Acts. Share your faith simply where you now live.
Look for the grace of God in someone else's work this week and tell them so. Encouragement is a ministry.
Think of someone gifted but kept at a distance. Introduce them, include them, give them a chance to serve.
When you are anxious tonight, open your hand and pray: “No one will snatch me out of your hand, Lord.”
fathers: Hear “one,” and be delivered from Arius, who denied that the Son is equal to the Father; hear “are,” and be delivered from Sabellius, who denied that the Father and the Son are distinct. The Father and I are one: one in substance, yet truly two persons.
It is right not only to be called Christians but to be Christians in truth. Christianity is not a matter of persuasive words but of greatness, when it is hated by the world.
Barnabas came, saw, and rejoiced; he was not jealous that the work had begun without him. This is the mark of a good man: to be glad at the good done by others.
magis: The Trinity is one: the divine persons do not share the one divinity among themselves, but each is God whole and entire; and they are really distinct from one another.
The Council of Nicaea confessed the Son consubstantial with the Father.
The pilgrim Church is missionary by her very nature.
The Church rejects any charge against the Jewish people as a whole for the death of Christ and decries every form of antisemitism.
The name “Christian” means “anointed” and comes from the name of Christ himself.
saints: Dominican prioress in Tuscany (died 20 April 1317), known for her prayer, her love of poverty and her gift of peace-making. St Catherine of Siena made a pilgrimage to her tomb. The Roman Martyrology commemorates her today.
21 Apr: St Anselm. 23 Apr: St George; St Adalbert. 24 Apr: St Fidelis. 25 Apr: Fifth Sunday of Easter.
2027-04-20.prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, Good Shepherd, one with the Father, you know your sheep and give them eternal life, and no one can snatch them out of your hand. Make us worthy of the name Christian, which we have received from you. Give us the courage of the scattered disciples who spoke of you wherever they went, and the generous heart of Barnabas, who rejoiced to see your grace at work in others. Keep us in your hand in every danger, and bring us at last into the joy of the Father, with whom you live and reign in the unity of the Holy Spirit, God, for ever and ever. Alleluia. Amen.

quick: The scattered believers proclaimed Jesus to the Gentiles of Antioch.

Jesus: My sheep hear my voice; no one will snatch them out of my hand; the Father and I are one.
2027-04-20.action: Encourage one person today by naming something good God is doing through them.
2027-04-20.question: If my neighbours had to give me a name from the way I live, would they call me a Christian?
catechism: The Trinity is one God in three persons.
The Son consubstantial with the Father.
“Christian” means anointed, from the name of Christ.
kidsaint: Barnabas's name means “son of encouragement.” When everybody was afraid of Saul, who used to hurt Christians, Barnabas became his friend and brought him to Antioch. Together they taught many people about Jesus. Lesson: we can be like Barnabas when we encourage others and help them feel welcome.
2027-04-20.special: Easter weekday: Regina Caeli at noon; Alleluia in the antiphons.
term: From the Latin consubstantialis, translating the Greek homoousios, “of the same substance” or “one in being.” The Creed says the Son is consubstantial with the Father: not a creature, but God from God, light from light.

family.explain: Jesus says his sheep know his voice and follow him. He gives them life that never ends, and he holds them so tightly in his hand that nobody can take them away. And his hand is the same as the Father's hand, because Jesus and the Father are one.
family.intention: We pray for all who are afraid or in danger, that they may feel safe in Jesus' hand.
family.ask: Ask: “What does it mean that our family's name is ‘Christian’?” Make the Sign of the Cross together slowly, remembering whose people we are.

illus: A young nurse from Kottayam went to work in a hospital in Riyadh, where there was no parish she could visit openly. At first she felt she had left the Church behind. Then she began to pray the Rosary each night with two Filipino nurses and a Kenyan cleaner in her building. A year later there were fourteen of them, quietly reading the Sunday Gospel together. When she came home on leave, she told her parish priest: I thought I was scattered, but I was being sown.

pm.open: Lord Jesus, Good Shepherd, we hear your voice; hold us in your hand and send us out to speak your name. Alleluia. Amen.
share: The hand of the Lord was with them (Acts 11:21). Where have I seen God's hand in the spread of the faith?
When he came and saw the grace of God, he rejoiced (Acts 11:23). Whose good work can I rejoice in and encourage?
No one will snatch them out of my hand (John 10:28). What fear do I need to place in the hand of Jesus?
pm.resp: All you nations, praise the Lord.
interc: For Christians scattered by work, migration or persecution, that they may be seeds of the Gospel wherever they live.
For the persecuted Church, that the Lord may hold her in his hand.
For pastors and leaders, that like Barnabas they may see grace and encourage it.
For our Jewish brothers and sisters, the first to hear the word of God, that they may be blessed in faithfulness to his covenant.
For our group, that we may truly deserve the name Christian.
pm.close: Father, your Son holds his sheep in your hand. Keep us faithful to him and make us bearers of his name to all peoples. Through Christ our Lord. Amen.

homily: Dear friends, after Stephen was killed, the believers ran away from Jerusalem. It looked like the end. But Luke tells us that wherever they went, they spoke about Jesus. They were scattered like seed, and the seed grew.

In Antioch some unnamed believers did something new: they told the Greeks about the Lord Jesus. And the hand of the Lord was with them (Acts 11:21). Many of us, too, have been scattered, to the Gulf, to Europe, to other states. God can use our scattering to sow his word.

Then the Church sends Barnabas. Luke says he was a good man, full of the Holy Spirit and of faith. When he saw the grace of God, he rejoiced (Acts 11:23). He did not complain that things were done without his permission. He rejoiced, and he encouraged.

And he went to look for Saul, a man others were afraid of. He gave him a place. Together they taught for a whole year, and in Antioch the disciples were first called Christians. That is our name too. Do we live up to it?

In the Gospel Jesus says: my sheep hear my voice; I know them, and they follow me. I give them eternal life, and they will never perish. No one will snatch them out of my hand (John 10:27–28). Whatever storms we face, we are held. And the hand that holds us is the Father's hand, for Jesus says: the Father and I are one.
Today let us be Barnabas for someone: let us see grace and rejoice. And let us rest in the hand of the Shepherd, from which no one can snatch us. Alleluia. Amen.
kids: Children, Jesus says he holds his sheep in his hand, so tightly that no one can take them away. You are in Jesus' hand!
At Antioch the friends of Jesus were first called Christians. That is your name too. Let us say: Jesus, I belong to you!

intro: Scattered believers who sowed the word, Barnabas who rejoiced in grace, and the Shepherd's hand that no one can open.

When he came and saw the grace of God, he rejoiced, and he exhorted them all to remain faithful to the Lord with steadfast devotion;

sub: They hear, he knows, they follow.
The Father and I are one.
q: For thus says the Lord God: I myself will search for my sheep, and will seek them out.
My sheep hear my voice. I know them, and they follow me.
points.apply: Each night this week, place your biggest worry in the hand of Jesus with one sentence of trust.

concl: God turned the scattering of his people into the sowing of his word, and at Antioch they were first called Christians.
Christ, one with the Father, holds his sheep so firmly that no one can snatch them from his hand.
2027-04-20.resolve: Live this week so that your name, Christian, is true.
